Guided Inquiry

1. Fire straight up, just below escape

The launch speed is set to 10.5 km/s from Earth's surface — just under escape speed. The angle is 90° (straight up). Press ▶ Play and watch the projectile. Does it leave and never return, or come back?

2. Predict — same speed, tilted to 45°

Keep the launch speed at 10.5 km/s, but tilt the launcher to 45°. Does the projectile now escape?

3. Watch the 45° launch

The launcher is now at 45°. Press ▶ Play. Watch the path — and the energy bar, now on the right. Does the sign of E change when only the direction changes?

4. Predict — a marble vs a spaceship

A 1 g marble and a 1000 t spaceship both launch straight up from Earth. Which needs the higher launch speed to escape?

5. Cross the threshold

The speed slider and readouts are now live. Push v₀ up through the vesc mark on the slider and watch KE + PE. Where does the total-energy sign flip, and does the path stop coming back?

Then try the Moon and Jupiter. Does vesc / vcirc stay √2 on every world?

01

At a glance

A projectile is fired from the surface of a planet, and the sim draws its path beside a bar chart of its energy per kilogram. You choose the launch and the world, and the sim shows what becomes of the projectile.

What you'll learn

  • What decides whether a projectile launched from a planet ever comes back.
  • How kinetic and potential energy per kilogram add up to a total that can be negative or positive.
  • Where the formula for escape speed comes from, and how it compares with the speed of a circular orbit.
The projectile starts on the surface with speed v₀, at an angle θ above the local horizon.

What's on screen

  • Planet and projectile: a side view of the planet with an amber launcher arrow on its surface. The pink dot is the projectile, and the line behind it is its path.
  • Energy per kg (right panel): bars for KE, PE and the total E, in MJ/kg.
  • Captions: the planet and the state of the launch at the bottom left, and the launch speed at the bottom right.
See itFire from Earth at the opening 10.5 km/s, straight up. Watch for: the pink dot leaving the amber launcher, with a blue line growing behind it as it climbs.

03

The sign of the total energy decides the launch

For a projectile at distance r from the centre of a planet of mass M, the energy per kilogram is the kinetic part plus the potential part:

E = ½v² − GM/r
KE per kg is ½v². PE per kg is −GM/r, which is zero at infinite distance.

Gravity is the only force, so E stays the same all along the flight. Its sign sorts every launch:

  • E < 0: the projectile is bound. It climbs to a greatest distance and comes back.
  • E ≥ 0: the projectile is unbound. It never returns.

At 10.5 km/s from Earth's surface, KE = 55.13 and PE = −62.57 MJ/kg, so E = −7.44 MJ/kg. The E bar is amber when E is negative and green when it is not.

See itFire from Earth at 10.5 km/s, straight up. Watch for: KE falling and PE rising as the dot climbs, E staying at −7.44 MJ/kg, and the caption fell back to surface.
04

The escape speed makes the total energy zero

The borderline launch has E = 0 at the surface, where r is the planet's radius. Then ½v² = GM/r, and

vesc = √(2GM/r)
Any launch speed from vesc upwards has E ≥ 0.

The mass of the projectile cancelled, because E is already per kilogram. A 1 g marble and a 1000 t spaceship need the same speed from the same place, although the spaceship needs a billion times more energy in joules.

For Earth, r = 6371 km and GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² give vesc = 11.19 km/s. So a launch at 10.5 km/s is below the threshold, and a launch at 11.3 km/s is above it.

See itRaise the launch speed to 11.3 km/s, straight up from Earth. Watch for: the E bar turning green at +1.28 MJ/kg, and the caption escaped — never returns.
05

Tilting the launch does not change the energy

E = ½v² − GM/r contains the speed v and the distance r, and no direction. Launch from the same surface point at the same speed, and E is the same at every angle. So:

  • A launch that falls back when fired straight up also falls back at 45°.
  • A launch above vesc escapes at every angle the sim allows, 5° to 90°.

The angle changes the shape of the path, not the verdict. At 10.5 km/s from Earth, straight up reaches about 8.4 planet radii from the centre, and 45° reaches about 7.9. Aiming does not give a bound projectile more energy. It only changes where the projectile goes while bound.

See itTilt the launch to 45° at 10.5 km/s. Watch for: a curved path that closes back on the planet, with E still −7.44 MJ/kg.
06

Escape speed is √2 times the circular-orbit speed

A satellite circling just above the surface has gravity as its centripetal force: GM/r² = v²/r. So vcirc = √(GM/r). Compare this with vesc = √(2GM/r):

vesc / vcirc = √2 ≈ 1.41421
Both speeds contain √(GM/r), so the ratio is the same at every radius.
Worldvcircvesc
Earth7.91 km/s11.19 km/s
Moon1.68 km/s2.38 km/s
Jupiter42.57 km/s60.21 km/s

A body already skimming the surface in a circular orbit needs only about 41% more speed to escape.

See itSwitch to the Moon and launch at 2.5 km/s. Watch for: the Readouts panel showing vesc = 2.38 and vcirc = 1.68 km/s, with the same ratio √2 = 1.41421 as on Earth.
07

Where it matters

  • Atmospheres. A planet holds a gas only if its molecules move much slower than vesc. The Moon's 2.38 km/s is one reason it has almost no atmosphere. At the same temperature, light hydrogen and helium move faster than heavy nitrogen, so Earth loses them over time while keeping the nitrogen.
  • Rockets. A rocket does not have to reach vesc at launch, because its engines keep adding energy. The escape speed describes a body that is thrown and then only coasts.
  • Energy cost. Escaping Earth takes ½vesc² = 62.56 MJ for each kilogram, which is the same as GM/r at the surface.
  • Earth's spin. Near the equator the ground already moves east at about 0.46 km/s, which helps an eastward launch. The sim leaves this out.
08

Summary

In one line. Whether a launch from a planet ever returns is settled by its total energy per kilogram, E = ½v² − GM/r.

Key points

  • E < 0 means bound and E ≥ 0 means unbound, and E does not change during the flight.
  • Setting E = 0 at the surface gives vesc = √(2GM/r).
  • The projectile's mass and the launch angle do not enter the escape speed.
  • vesc = √2 × vcirc at every radius, on every planet.

Common mix-ups

  • "A heavier rocket needs a higher escape speed." The speed is the same. Only the energy in joules grows with the mass.
  • "Tilting to 45° gives more range, so it escapes." The energy is the same at every angle. More range does not mean E ≥ 0.
  • "At escape speed gravity stops pulling." Gravity never switches off. At exactly vesc the speed shrinks and reaches zero only at infinite distance.

Things to try on your own

  • On Earth, raise the launch speed in 0.05 km/s steps and find where the E bar first turns green. Compare that speed with 11.19 km/s.
  • On the Moon at 45°, launch at 2.3 km/s and then at 2.5 km/s, and compare the two outcomes with the Moon's 2.38 km/s.
  • On Jupiter, find the smallest launch speed that escapes, then divide it by the vcirc readout.
